props.title: Harold and Maude
props.initialSlug: Young man finds joy through elderly free spirit's love

sections.content: Harold and Maude (1971) revolutionized dark comedy by pairing a death-obsessed 20-year-old with a free-spirited 79-year-old woman. Director Hal Ashby crafted an unlikely love story that thumbs its nose at social conventions while celebrating life's absurdities. The film's influence echoes through later unconventional romances like Rushmore (1998) and Garden State (2004). Cat Stevens' folk soundtrack perfectly captures both Harold's melancholy and Maude's joie de vivre, establishing a template for indie film soundtracks that directors like Wes Anderson would later embrace.

sections.content: The film's treatment of death and suicide broke new ground in American cinema. While earlier films treated death with somber reverence, Harold's elaborate fake suicides turn mortality into dark comedy. This influenced later films like Heathers (1988) and World's Greatest Dad (2009), which similarly mine uncomfortable subjects for bitter laughs. Ashby's direction maintains perfect tonal balance - never letting the film slip into pure farce or melodrama.

Bud Cort and Ruth Gordon's performances create an unlikely chemistry that makes their May-December romance believable and touching rather than creepy. Their relationship laid groundwork for other age-gap romances like Lost in Translation (2003) and The Graduate (1967), though Harold and Maude remains the most extreme and effective example. The film's anti-establishment themes perfectly captured the countercultural spirit of the early 1970s while remaining timeless. SUBHEAD: Cultural Impact and Legacy

sections.content: Harold and Maude initially flopped but found its audience through midnight screenings, similar to The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975). Its influence extends beyond film into music - The Smiths and other artists reference it frequently. Modern filmmakers like Sofia Coppola and Paul Thomas Anderson cite it as a major influence, particularly in how it balances comedy and tragedy. The film's success in handling taboo subjects paved the way for other dark comedies like Welcome to the Dollhouse (1995) and Napoleon Dynamite (2004).
